G1.why: Meinungsfreiheit is protected by Art. 5 GG, so criticising the government publicly is allowed.
G1.trap: The Wahlrecht option sounds democratic, but voting is not what the question asks about.
G1.trick: Five fingers on a megaphone: Art. 5 = free speech.

G2.why: Art. 7(2) GG lets parents decide whether their child attends Religionsunterricht; from age 14 the child decides its religion itself.
G2.trap: Geschichtsunterricht or Politikunterricht may sound optional, but they are normal compulsory subjects.
G2.trick: Religion is the only subject you can opt out of: 14 = the child takes over.

G3.why: In a Rechtsstaat everyone, including the state itself, is bound by the law (Art. 20(3) GG).
G3.trap: 'Die Gerichte machen die Gesetze' is wrong: parliament makes laws, courts apply them.
G3.trick: Rechtsstaat = nobody stands above the law, not even the state.

G4.why: Meinungsfreiheit is a basic right in Art. 5 GG.
G4.trap: Waffenbesitz sounds like a right because the US constitution has one, but the Grundgesetz does not.
G4.trick: Speech yes, weapons no: Germany is not the USA.

G5.why: A free election means nobody may pressure, bribe or force you how to vote, and voting must not harm you (Art. 38(1) GG).
G5.trap: 'Alle müssen wählen' is wrong: there is no compulsory voting in Germany, and 'free' includes the freedom not to vote.
G5.trick: Free vote = no pressure, no payment, no punishment.

G6.why: The German constitution is called the Grundgesetz; it was signed and announced on 23 May 1949.
G6.trap: 'Bundesgesetz' sounds official, but that is just the term for any ordinary federal law.
G6.trick: Grund = foundation: the Grundgesetz is the foundation of all other laws.

G7.why: Freedom of faith and conscience (Glaubens- und Gewissensfreiheit) is guaranteed in Art. 4 GG.
G7.trap: A right to Arbeit or Wohnung sounds social, but the Grundgesetz does not guarantee a job or a flat.
G7.trick: Art. 4 = faith: believe what you want, 4 ever.

G8.why: The Grundgesetz guarantees equality before the law, not equal income, so 'everyone should have the same money' is not in it.
G8.trap: 'Jeder Mensch darf seine Meinung sagen' may look too casual to be constitutional, but it is Art. 5 GG.

G9.why: Asylum is a right for people persecuted for political reasons (Art. 16a GG), and German citizens cannot claim asylum in their own country.
G9.trap: Schutz der Familie may sound like a special protection, but Art. 6 GG protects every family, German or not.
G9.trick: Asyl is only for people who come from outside.

G10.why: A fine (Geldstrafe) is a normal criminal penalty; the other options violate human dignity.
G10.trap: Todesstrafe may seem possible for the worst crimes, but Art. 102 GG says: 'Die Todesstrafe ist abgeschafft.'

G11.why: The constitution of the Federal Republic is called the Grundgesetz.
G11.trap: 'Bundesverfassung' sounds logical (Switzerland's constitution has that name), but Germany's is the Grundgesetz.

G12.why: Press freedom is a basic right (Art. 5(1) GG), and basic rights are protected against being removed by a parliamentary majority.
G12.trap: The two-thirds option is tempting because changing the Grundgesetz needs two thirds, but that would also need the Bundesrat (Art. 79(2) GG) and the official answer is that a basic right cannot simply be abolished.
G12.trick: Basic rights are locked: no vote opens the lock.

G13.why: The opposition is every member of parliament who does not belong to the governing party or parties.
G13.trap: 'Die Fraktion mit den meisten Abgeordneten' is wrong: the biggest group usually leads the government, not the opposition.

G14.why: Free speech (Art. 5 GG) covers posting your opinion online.
G14.trap: Wearing Nazi, Hamas or IS symbols is not free speech; showing them in public is a crime in Germany.
G14.trick: Opinion online: yes. Insults or extremist symbols: no.

G15.why: The Grundgesetz forbids forced labour (Art. 12 GG); it is only allowed as part of a prison sentence ordered by a court.
G15.trap: Militärdienst is tempting, but the Grundgesetz allows it (Art. 12a GG lets men be called up for military service).
G15.trick: Free Berufswahl, no Zwangsarbeit: you choose your work.

G16.why: Free speech has limits where it hurts other people: spreading false factual claims about a person can be a crime (üble Nachrede, Verleumdung).
G16.trap: 'Kritik am Staat' may sound risky, but criticising the state is exactly what free speech protects.
G16.trick: Criticise the state freely, but don't lie about people.

G17.why: Art. 3 GG says everyone is equal before the law, so the state may not treat citizens unequally.
G17.trap: Petitionen might sound like something the state could limit, but Art. 17 GG gives everyone the right to send petitions.
G17.trick: The state must treat all citizens equally: Art. 3 = equality.

G18.why: Art. 1(1) GG says: 'Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar.'
G18.trap: Das Recht auf Leben is a basic right too, but it is in Art. 2 GG, not Art. 1.
G18.trick: Number 1 comes first: human dignity is Art. 1.

G19.why: Freizügigkeit (Art. 11 GG) is the right of Germans to choose where they live and to move freely anywhere in Germany.
G19.trap: Changing your job is a different right, Berufsfreiheit in Art. 12 GG.
G19.trick: Frei + Zug: free to move house.

G20.why: A party that wants to set up a dictatorship fights the free democratic order and is therefore unconstitutional (Art. 21(2) GG).
G20.trap: 'Gesetzestreu' may look neutral, but a party aiming for dictatorship acts against the constitution, the highest law.

G21.why: Bild 1 shows the Bundesadler, the black eagle with red beak and claws on a gold shield, which is the federal coat of arms.
G21.trap: Bild 4 is tempting because it uses black, red and gold, but it is the coat of arms of the former DDR (hammer and compass).
G21.trick: Germany's coat of arms is an eagle, not a tool.

G22.why: Germany is a republic: the head of state is an elected president, not a king (Art. 20(1) GG).
G22.trap: Monarchie is tempting because Germany had an emperor until 1918, but that ended with the Weimar Republic.

G23.why: Most working people in Germany are employees of a company or a public authority.
G23.trap: Family businesses are common, but most workers are employees of a company or authority, not of a small family business.
G23.trick: Most Germans are Angestellte, not Chefs.

G24.why: Germany has 16 Bundesländer since reunification in 1990.
G24.trap: 15 is tempting if you forget that the city-states Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen count as Länder too.
G24.trick: Brandenburg lets 16-year-olds vote for the Landtag, and Germany has 16 Länder.

G25.why: Elsass-Lothringen (Alsace-Lorraine) is a region of France; it belonged to the German Empire only from 1871 to 1918.
G25.trap: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Sachsen-Anhalt sound unusual, but both are real Bundesländer in the east.

G26.why: Art. 20(1) GG: 'Die Bundesrepublik Deutschland ist ein demokratischer und sozialer Bundesstaat.'
G26.trap: 'Sozialer und sozialistischer Bundesstaat' is tempting because 'sozial' is right, but Germany is not socialist.
G26.trick: Learn Art. 20(1) by heart: demokratisch, sozial, Bundesstaat.

G27.why: Germany is a Bundesstaat, a federal state made up of 16 Länder (Art. 20(1) GG).
G27.trap: Monarchie is tempting for historical reasons, but Germany has been a republic since 1918/19.

G28.why: The members of the Bundestag are elected by the people who have the right to vote (Art. 38(1) GG).
G28.trap: 'Die Verwaltung' is wrong: public administration runs elections, but it does not choose who wins.

G29.why: The Bundesadler (eagle) is Germany's heraldic animal.
G29.trap: Bär is tempting because it is Berlin's symbol, but that is the city's coat of arms, not the federal one.
G29.trick: Adler for the Bund, Bär for Berlin.

G30.why: Press censorship is not part of a democracy; Art. 5(1) GG says 'Eine Zensur findet nicht statt.'
G30.trap: Verschiedene Parteien might look optional, but a one-party state is not a democracy, so it is a real feature.
G30.trick: Democracy has a free press, never a censor.

G31.why: When several parties work together to form a government, it is called a Koalition.
G31.trap: Fraktion is tempting because it is also a group in parliament, but a Fraktion is the members of one party (or allied parties like CDU/CSU), not a government alliance.

G32.why: The three state powers are legislation, executive (including the government) and judiciary (Art. 20(2) GG); the press is not a state power.
G32.trap: Regierung is tempting because it sounds different from the classic three, but the government is part of the executive.
G32.trick: The press watches the state but is not the state.

G33.why: State and religious communities are separate in Germany; there is no state church (Art. 140 GG with Art. 137 WRV).
G33.trap: 'Staat und Religionsgemeinschaften bilden eine Einheit' may seem plausible because of church tax and religion classes, but they remain separate institutions.
G33.trick: No state church: church and state are separate.

G34.why: Germany is a democracy, a Rechtsstaat and a Sozialstaat, but not a monarchy.
G34.trap: Sozialstaat may sound like a political goal rather than a fact, but Art. 20(1) GG makes Germany a social state.
G34.trick: Three yes, one no: no king, no Monarchie.

G35.why: Social insurance is mainly paid for by Sozialabgaben, contributions taken from wages and mostly shared by employees and employers.
G35.trap: Kirchensteuer is tempting because the state collects it, but the money goes to the churches, not to social insurance.

G36.why: Health insurance is part of the social insurance system and protects people when they are ill.
G36.trap: Autoversicherung is tempting because liability cover for a car is compulsory, but it is private insurance for vehicle damage, not social security.
G36.trick: Social security protects people; car insurance protects cars.

G37.why: The heads of government of most Länder are called Ministerpräsidentin or Ministerpräsident.
G37.trap: Senatorin/Senator is tempting because the city-states use that word, but there Senators are ministers, and the head is a Bürgermeister.
G37.trick: Most Länder have a Ministerpräsident; only Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen have a Bürgermeister at the top.

G38.why: Art. 20(1) GG calls Germany 'ein demokratischer und sozialer Bundesstaat'.
G38.trap: Staatenbund is tempting, but that is a loose confederation of independent states, not one federal state.
G38.trick: Same sentence as Question 26: demokratisch, sozial, Bundesstaat.

G39.why: Every Land has its own parliament (Landtag) and its own government.
G39.trap: Eine eigene Währung is wrong: all Länder use the euro.
G39.trick: Länder have their own governments, but share the army, the euro and foreign policy.

G40.why: The national anthem is the third verse of the Deutschlandlied and starts with 'Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit'.
G40.trap: 'Deutschland einig Vaterland' sounds German, but it is a line from the DDR anthem.
G40.trick: Unity, justice, freedom: the anthem opens with three values.

G41.why: Several parties are needed so that the different opinions of the citizens are represented.
G41.trap: 'Um wirtschaftlichen Wettbewerb anzuregen' is tempting because competition sounds good, but parties compete for political ideas, not for the economy.

G42.why: Federal laws are passed by parliament: Art. 77(1) GG says 'Die Bundesgesetze werden vom Bundestage beschlossen.'
G42.trap: Die Regierung is tempting because it proposes most bills, but it cannot pass a law itself.

G43.why: A party can be banned if it fights against the free democratic order; only the Bundesverfassungsgericht can decide this (Art. 21 GG).
G43.trap: 'Wenn sie Kritik am Staatsoberhaupt äußert' is wrong: criticising the president is allowed political speech.
G43.trick: Only fighting the constitution gets a party banned.

G44.why: The Bundespräsident is elected by the Bundesversammlung, not directly by the people (Art. 54 GG).
G44.trap: EU-Parlament may sound distant, but Germans elect its members directly in European elections.
G44.trick: The President is chosen by the Bundesversammlung, never by voters directly.

G45.why: Long-term care insurance (Pflegeversicherung) is one of the branches of the statutory social insurance, introduced in 1995.
G45.trap: Unfallversicherung is tempting because statutory accident insurance is also social insurance, but Pflegeversicherung is its own branch, not part of it.
G45.trick: Pflege belongs to the social family: health, pension, unemployment, accident, care.

G46.why: Building roads and schools is public infrastructure, a typical task of the state.
G46.trap: 'Er produziert Autos und Busse' may seem plausible for public transport, but cars and buses are made by private companies.
G46.trick: The state builds what everyone uses: roads and schools.

G47.why: The state does not pay for holidays; it does pay Kindergeld, support museums and promote sport.
G47.trap: Fördert Sportlerinnen und Sportler may sound like a luxury, but the state does fund sport, for example top athletes in the Bundeswehr or federal police.

G48.why: The constitutional bodies include the Bundestag, Bundesrat, Bundespräsident, Bundesregierung and Bundesverfassungsgericht; a Bürgerversammlung is not one of them.
G48.trap: Bürgerversammlung is easy to mix up with the Bundesversammlung, which is a constitutional body (it elects the President).

G49.why: School policy is mainly the responsibility of the Bundesländer (Kulturhoheit der Länder).
G49.trap: Das Familienministerium is tempting because schools concern families, but the federal government has little say over schools.

G50.why: Germany's economic system is the soziale Marktwirtschaft: a free market with social protection, shaped by Ludwig Erhard.
G50.trap: Planwirtschaft is tempting if you think of the DDR, but that system ended with reunification.

G51.why: In a Rechtsstaat nobody may be locked up without a legal reason, and only a judge may decide on longer detention (Art. 104 GG); a private police force has no such power.
G51.trap: 'Jemand begeht ein Verbrechen und wird deshalb verhaftet' may look like a restriction of freedom, but arresting a suspect lawfully is normal in a Rechtsstaat.
G51.trick: No private police, no arrest without reason.

G52.why: Art. 20(2) GG: 'Alle Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus.'
G52.trap: Bundestag is tempting because it holds a lot of power, but it only exercises the power the people give it in elections.

G53.why: Rechtsstaat means the state itself must obey the law (Art. 20(3) GG).
G53.trap: 'Der Staat hat Recht' plays on the word Recht, but the term means the state is bound by law, not that it is always right.
G53.trick: Rechtsstaat = the state follows the law, not the other way round.

G54.why: The three state powers are Legislative, Exekutive and Judikative; 'Direktive' is not one of them.
G54.trap: Legislative, Judikative and Exekutive all sound equally Latin, so the trap is the made-up word that sounds just like them.
G54.trick: L-E-J are the three real powers; anything else is invented.

G55.why: The picture shows the Reichstag building with its glass dome, the seat of the Bundestag in Berlin.
G55.trap: Das Bundesratsgebäude in Berlin is tempting because it is also a historic building in Berlin, but it has no glass dome.

G56.why: The Ordnungsamt is part of the town or municipal administration and deals with local public order, for example parking control and noise complaints.
G56.trap: Finanzamt is tempting because it is a local office, but it belongs to the Land, not to the municipality.
G56.trick: The town has an Ordnungsamt, the Land a Finanzamt, the Bund an Auswärtiges Amt.

G57.why: By tradition the strongest parliamentary group (Fraktion) proposes the President of the Bundestag, who is a member of that group.
G57.trap: The oldest member is tempting, but the Alterspräsident only opens the first session; since 2017 that role goes to the longest-serving member.
G57.trick: The biggest group gets the chair.

G58.why: The Bundespräsident appoints the federal ministers on the proposal of the Chancellor (Art. 64(1) GG).
G58.trap: Die Bundestagspräsidentin/der Bundestagspräsident sounds powerful, but that office runs parliament and does not appoint ministers.

G59.why: A decree of Emperor Constantine from the year 321 is the earliest record of Jews in Cologne, about 1700 years ago; Germany marked '1700 Jahre jüdisches Leben' in 2021.
G59.trap: 'Vor etwa 700 Jahren' is tempting if you think of the medieval Jewish communities, but Jewish life in the region is much older.

G60.why: Bundestag and Bundesrat are the legislative bodies: they make the federal laws together.
G60.trap: Exekutive is tempting because the Bundesrat is made up of members of the Land governments, but as a body it takes part in lawmaking.

G61.why: Volkssouveränität means all state power comes from the people (Art. 20(2) GG).
G61.trap: 'Das Bundesverfassungsgericht steht über der Verfassung' is wrong: the court protects the constitution and is bound by it.
G61.trick: Volk + Souverän: the people are the boss.

G62.why: The parliament of a Bundesland is the Landtag, so its election is a Landtagswahl; Brandenburg last voted in September 2024.
G62.trap: Kommunalwahl is tempting because it is also regional, but it elects town and district councils, not the state parliament.

G63.why: Courts belong to the judiciary (Judikative), not to the executive.
G63.trap: Das Finanzamt may not feel like 'government', but as a public authority it is part of the executive.
G63.trick: Executive executes (police, ministries, offices); courts judge.

G64.why: Germany is organised on three levels: the federation (Bund), the 16 Länder and the municipalities (Kommunen).
G64.trap: 16 Kantone is tempting because the number 16 is right, but Kantone are the member states of Switzerland.
G64.trick: Bund, Land, Kommune: three floors of one house.

G65.why: The Bundestag does not form the cabinet: the Chancellor chooses the ministers and the Bundespräsident appoints them (Art. 64(1) GG).
G65.trap: 'Gesetze zu entwerfen' is tempting, but members of the Bundestag can introduce bills themselves (Art. 76(1) GG), so it is one of its tasks.
G65.trick: Bundestag elects the Chancellor; the Chancellor builds the cabinet.

G66.why: Berlin and München (Munich) have the largest Jewish communities in Germany today.
G66.trap: Worms and Speyer are tempting because they are famous historic Jewish centres (the medieval SchUM cities), but today their communities are small.
G66.trick: Biggest cities, biggest communities: Berlin and München.

G67.why: Education and schools are mainly the responsibility of the Länder.
G67.trap: Wirtschaftspolitik is tempting because the Länder do promote their regional economy, but economic policy is mostly made at federal and EU level.
G67.trick: Defence and foreign policy for the Bund, schools for the Länder.

G68.why: Art. 7(1) GG puts the whole school system under the supervision of the state.
G68.trap: 'Weil es nur staatliche Schulen gibt' is wrong: private schools exist and are allowed (Art. 7(4) GG), they are just supervised.
G68.trick: Art. 7 = school: the state watches over all schools.

G69.why: The lowest political level of Germany's three-level structure (Bund, Länder, Kommunen) is the municipality, the Gemeinde.
G69.trap: Landräte is tempting, but a Landrat is a person, the head of a Landkreis, not an administrative level.
G69.trick: Bund at the top, Land in the middle, Gemeinde at the bottom.

G70.why: The Bundespräsident proposes a candidate for Chancellor, and the Bundestag then elects that person (Art. 63(1) GG).
G70.trap: 'Sie/Er wählt die Ministerinnen/Minister aus' is tempting because the President formally appoints ministers, but the Chancellor chooses them.
G70.trick: President proposes and hands over the certificate; the Bundestag elects.

G71.why: The Chancellor works mostly in Berlin, where the Federal Chancellery (Bundeskanzleramt) and the Bundestag are.
G71.trap: Bonn is tempting because it was the seat of government until the move to Berlin in 1999, but the Chancellery and the Bundestag are now in Berlin.
G71.trick: Bonn was then, Berlin is now.

G72.why: As of October 2026, Friedrich Merz (CDU) is Federal Chancellor; he was elected by the Bundestag on 6 May 2025. Check before the test.
G72.trap: Angela Merkel is tempting because she was Chancellor for 16 years, but she left office in 2021.
G72.trick: Merz since May 2025: M for Merz, M for May.

G73.why: As of October 2026, CDU/CSU (208 seats) and AfD (150 seats, after two members left) are the two largest groups in the Bundestag elected in February 2025. Check before the test.
G73.trap: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen und SPD is tempting if you remember the previous government, but after the 2025 election the SPD is third and the Greens fourth.

G74.why: The national parliament for all of Germany is the Bundestag.
G74.trap: Volkskammer is tempting because it sounds like a people's parliament, but it was the parliament of the former DDR.
G74.trick: Bundestag for the Bund, Landtag for the Land.

G75.why: As of October 2026, Frank-Walter Steinmeier is head of state; his second and last term ends on 18 March 2027, and his successor will be elected on 30 January 2027, so he is still in office on 8 Dec 2026. Check before the test.
G75.trap: Joachim Gauck is tempting because he was Bundespräsident, but he served from 2012 to 2017, before Steinmeier.

G76.why: CDU stands for Christlich Demokratische Union.
G76.trap: 'Christliche Deutsche Union' is tempting because 'Deutschland' fits, but the D stands for 'Demokratische'.

G77.why: The Bundeswehr is Germany's armed forces, founded in 1955.
G77.trap: 'Die deutsche Polizei' is tempting because both wear uniforms, but police and army are separate institutions.

G78.why: SPD stands for Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands.
G78.trap: 'Sozialistische Partei Deutschlands' is tempting because the letters match, but the SPD is social democratic, not socialist.

G79.why: FDP stands for Freie Demokratische Partei.
G79.trap: 'Freie Deutschland Partei' is tempting because the F and P fit, but the D stands for 'Demokratische'.
G79.trick: Most German party abbreviations hide a 'D' for 'Demokratisch'.

G80.why: The Bundesverfassungsgericht in Karlsruhe interprets the Grundgesetz (Art. 93 GG).
G80.trap: Oberlandesgericht is tempting because it sounds high, but it is a Land appeal court for civil and criminal cases.

G81.why: The Bundestag elects the Chancellor on the proposal of the Bundespräsident (Art. 63(1) GG).
G81.trap: 'Das Volk' is tempting because parties campaign with Chancellor candidates, but voters elect the Bundestag, not the Chancellor.
G81.trick: People elect the Bundestag; the Bundestag elects the Chancellor.

G82.why: The Chancellor leads the federal cabinet and sets its policy guidelines (Art. 65 GG).
G82.trap: Die Bundespräsidentin/der Bundespräsident is tempting because it is the highest office, but the President is not part of the government.
G82.trick: Kanzler leads the Kabinett: both start with K.

G83.why: The Bundestag elects the Chancellor (Art. 63(1) GG).
G83.trap: Die Bundesversammlung is tempting, but it elects the Bundespräsident, not the Chancellor.
G83.trick: Same as Question 81: Bundestag elects the Kanzler.

G84.why: The Bundespräsident's main task is to represent Germany; Art. 59(1) GG says the President represents the Federation in international law.
G84.trap: 'Überwacht die Einhaltung der Gesetze' is tempting because the President signs laws after checking how they were made, but enforcing laws is a job for authorities and courts.
G84.trick: The President represents; the Chancellor governs.

G85.why: The Bundesrat is made up of members of the governments of the Länder (Art. 51(1) GG).
G85.trap: 'Die Abgeordneten des Bundestages' is tempting because both are in Berlin, but the Bundesrat is a separate body.
G85.trick: Bundesrat = the Länder governments in Berlin.

G86.why: The Bundesversammlung elects the Bundespräsident; it consists of all members of the Bundestag plus the same number of delegates from the Landtage (Art. 54 GG).
G86.trap: Der Bundesrat is tempting because it also represents the Länder, but it has no role in electing the President.
G86.trick: Bundesversammlung: big assembly, one job, electing the President.

G87.why: The Bundespräsident is Germany's head of state.
G87.trap: Die Bundeskanzlerin/der Bundeskanzler is tempting because the Chancellor has the most political power, but heads the government, not the state.
G87.trick: Head of state = President; head of government = Chancellor.

G88.why: The opposition's main role is to control and criticise the government.
G88.trap: 'Entscheidet, wer Bundesministerin/Bundesminister wird' is wrong: the Chancellor picks the ministers.

G89.why: Members of parliament from one party (or allied parties like CDU and CSU) form a Fraktion.
G89.trap: Opposition is tempting because it is also a group of MPs, but it is all MPs outside the government, from several parties.
G89.trick: Fraktion = one party's team in parliament.

G90.why: The Länder take part in federal legislation through the Bundesrat (Art. 50 GG).
G90.trap: Die Bundesversammlung is tempting because it includes Land delegates, but it only meets to elect the President.
G90.trick: Länder have their say in the Bundesrat.

G91.why: A change of government in a Land can change the majority in the Bundesrat, and many federal laws need its consent, so governing becomes harder.
G91.trap: 'Wenn sich die Mehrheit im Bundestag ändert' is tempting, but a Land election does not change the Bundestag.
G91.trick: Land vote changes the Bundesrat, not the Bundestag.

G92.why: CSU stands for Christlich-Soziale Union; it exists only in Bavaria.
G92.trap: 'Christlich Süddeutsche Union' is tempting because the CSU is a southern party, but the S stands for 'Soziale'.
G92.trick: CDU everywhere except Bavaria; CSU only in Bavaria.

G93.why: The Zweitstimme decides the share of seats each party gets, so more Zweitstimmen means more seats.
G93.trap: 'Mehr Direktkandidaten' is tempting, but constituency candidates are chosen with the Erststimme.

G94.why: You can vote in the Bundestag election from age 18 (Art. 38(2) GG).
G94.trap: 16 is tempting because 16-year-olds can vote in European elections and in some Landtag elections, including Brandenburg, but not for the Bundestag.

G95.why: School is compulsory in Germany (Schulpflicht); the Länder regulate the details.
G95.trap: Wahlpflicht is tempting because it also ends in 'Pflicht', but there is no compulsory voting, and children cannot vote anyway.
G95.trick: Kids must go to school, not to the ballot box.

G96.why: Denying the Holocaust in public is a crime, punishable with up to five years in prison or a fine (§ 130(3) StGB).
G96.trap: 'Bis zu 100 Sozialstunden' is tempting because it sounds like a typical light penalty, but the law sets prison or a fine.

G97.why: For a regular employee, social insurance contributions are deducted automatically from the salary.
G97.trap: Sozialhilfe is tempting because it starts with 'Sozial', but it is a benefit you receive, not something you pay.
G97.trick: You pay Sozialversicherung; you receive Sozialhilfe, Kindergeld and Wohngeld.

G98.why: MPs keep their seat when they change group, because they are bound only by their conscience (Art. 38(1) GG), so a narrow government majority can be lost.
G98.trap: 'Dürfen nicht mehr an den Sitzungen teilnehmen' is wrong: the seat belongs to the MP, not to the party.

G99.why: Employers and employees share the cost of social insurance.
G99.trap: 'Nur Arbeitnehmer' is tempting because you see the deduction on your payslip, but your employer pays a similar share on top.
G99.trick: Social insurance is split: boss pays, worker pays.

G100.why: Life insurance is private, voluntary insurance and not part of statutory social insurance.

G101.why: Trade unions (Gewerkschaften) represent the interests of employees, for example in wage negotiations.

G102.why: The Bundesverdienstkreuz (Federal Cross of Merit) has honoured special achievements since 1951.

G103.why: The Ampelkoalition was SPD (red), FDP (yellow) and the Greens (green), like a traffic light; it governed under Olaf Scholz from 2021 to 2024.

G107.why: The Bundestag is elected for four years (Art. 39(1) GG).

G108.why: German citizens aged 18 or over may vote in the Bundestag election (Art. 38(2) GG).

G109.why: Bundestag elections are normally held every four years.

G110.why: The Bundestag is elected for four years (Art. 39(1) GG).
G110.trap: 5 Jahre is tempting because the European Parliament and most Landtage have five-year terms, but not the Bundestag.

G111.why: Publicly calling for the destruction of Israel is a crime, for example as incitement to hatred (Volksverhetzung).
G111.trap: 'Die Politik Israels öffentlich kritisieren' is tempting, but criticising a government's policy is protected free speech.
G111.trick: Criticism yes, calls for destruction no.

G112.why: Elections in Germany are secret: nobody may see or find out how you voted (Art. 38(1) GG).
G112.trap: 'Speziell' is the made-up distractor; the real principles are general, direct, free, equal and secret.

G113.why: The party with the most votes (Zweitstimmen) wins the election.
G113.trap: 'Die meisten Erststimmen für ihre Kanzlerkandidatin' is tempting, but the Chancellor is not directly elected and Erststimmen go to local candidates.

G114.why: Voting in Germany is a right, not a duty.
G114.trap: 'Eine Pflicht' is tempting because voting is a civic virtue, but nobody is fined or forced to vote.

G115.trap: 'Man kann gewählt werden' is tempting, but that is the passives Wahlrecht, the right to stand for election.
G115.trick: Active = you do the voting; passive = you get voted for.

G116.why: Being allowed to vote is called 'aktives Wahlrecht'.
G116.trap: Aktiver Wahlkampf is tempting, but a Wahlkampf is an election campaign.

G117.why: A party normally needs at least 5% of the Zweitstimmen to get seats in the Bundestag.
G117.trap: 3% is tempting because some countries use lower thresholds, but in Germany it is 5%.

G118.why: Makkabi sports clubs are open to everyone, regardless of religion or origin.
G118.trap: 'Nur religiöse Menschen' is tempting because the clubs are Jewish, but membership does not depend on faith.
G118.trick: Makkabi: Jewish roots, open to all.

G119.why: A free election means everyone decides without pressure whether to vote and whom to vote for.
G119.trap: 'Ich kann frei entscheiden, wo ich wählen gehen möchte' is tempting because of the word 'frei', but you vote at your assigned polling station (or by post).
G119.trick: Free = free from pressure, not free choice of polling station.

G120.why: Germany mixes majority voting (Erststimme for a constituency candidate) and proportional voting (Zweitstimme for a party list).
G120.trap: Dreiklassenwahlrecht is tempting because it sounds historical German, but it was Prussia's unequal system until 1918.
G120.trick: Two votes, two systems: Mehrheit + Verhältnis.

G121.why: The minimum share of votes a party needs to enter the Bundestag is called the 5%-Hürde.
G121.trap: Zulassungsgrenze is tempting because it sounds technical, but it is not the official term.
G121.trick: Hürde = hurdle: jump over 5% to get in.

G122.why: Art. 38(1) GG lists the principles: general, direct, free, equal and secret; 'frei, gleich, geheim' are three of them.
G122.trap: 'Offen, sicher, frei' is tempting because 'frei' is right, but elections are secret, not open.
G122.trick: Frei, gleich, geheim: three words for the ballot box.

G123.why: The 5%-Hürde is the minimum share of votes a party needs to get seats in parliament.
G123.trap: 'Abstimmungsregelung im Bundestag für kleine Parteien' is tempting, but the hurdle applies to elections, not to votes inside parliament.

G124.why: The Bundestag election chooses the federal parliament.
G124.trap: 'Der Bundeskanzlerin/des Bundeskanzlers' is tempting because campaigns focus on Chancellor candidates, but the Bundestag elects the Chancellor afterwards.

G125.why: Regular elections allow the government to change according to the will of the majority of voters.
G125.trap: 'Im Land bestehende Gesetze beizubehalten' is wrong: elections can lead to new laws, not just keep old ones.

G126.why: Before an election, voters receive a Wahlbenachrichtigung (polling card) from their municipality.
G126.trap: 'Eine Wahlerlaubnis vom Bundespräsidenten' is tempting because it sounds official, but nobody needs permission to vote.

G127.why: The 5%-Hürde exists because many small parties in parliament make it hard to form a stable government, as happened in the Weimar Republic.
G127.trap: 'Die Bürger verlieren die Orientierung' is tempting, but the reason is a stable parliament and government, not voter confusion.

G128.why: Members of parliament elected by the citizens are called Abgeordnete.
G128.trap: Ministerpräsidenten is tempting because they are also political leaders, but they are heads of Land governments, chosen by the Landtag.

G129.why: Of the options, only the Bundestag is elected directly by the people.

G129.trick: The people elect parliaments; parliaments elect leaders.

G130.why: Ballot 1 is valid because it has exactly one cross for a candidate (Erststimme) and one for a party (Zweitstimme); splitting them between parties is allowed.

G130.trick: One cross left, one cross right.

G131.why: A Bürgermeister is the head of a town or municipality (Gemeinde).
G131.trap: 'Die/der Vorsitzende einer Partei' is tempting because mayors are often party politicians, but leading a party is a different role.
G131.trick: Bürger + Meister = master of the citizens of a town.

G132.why: Ehrenamtlich means working voluntarily and unpaid, for example in clubs, associations or the volunteer fire brigade.

G132.trick: Ehrenamt = honour job: you get thanks, not pay.

G133.why: Postal voting (Briefwahl) is allowed in Bundestag and Landtag elections.
G133.trap: 'Der Ehemann wählt für seine Frau mit' may seem harmless, but every vote is personal and secret; nobody may vote for someone else.
G133.trick: No time on election day? Vote by post.

G134.why: Joining or founding a citizens' initiative (Bürgerinitiative) is a legal, democratic way to fight for a local cause like a bus line.

G135.trap: Selbstständige is tempting because they also work, but self-employed people are not employees and unions bargain with employers on behalf of staff.

G137.trap: Amtsgericht is tempting because it is the general local court, but labour disputes have their own court.
G137.trick: Same as Question 136: work goes to the Arbeitsgericht.

G138.why: Against an unfair dismissal you file a Kündigungsschutzklage at the labour court, normally within three weeks of receiving the notice.

G138.trick: Dismissed unfairly? Three weeks to sue.

G139.why: A criminal trial happens when someone is charged with a crime.
G139.trap: Wrong parking is tempting because you get towed and fined, but that is an administrative offence, normally without a trial.

G140.why: A Schöffe is a lay judge who decides on guilt and sentence together with professional judges.

G141.trick: Rechtsanwalt works for you; Staatsanwalt works for the state.

G142.why: A judge works at a court and delivers judgments.
G142.trap: 'Vertritt Bürgerinnen und Bürger vor einem Gericht' is tempting, but representing people is the lawyer's job; the judge must stay neutral.

G143.why: Judges belong to the judiciary, the Judikative.

G143.trick: Judge = Judikative: both start with J.

G144.why: Judges exercise the judicial power (rechtsprechende Gewalt) (Art. 92 GG).

G145.why: Judges work for the Judikative, the judicial branch of state power.

G145.trick: Same as Question 143: J for judge and Judikative.

G146.why: A court case is called a Prozess.

G147.why: A judge's work is 'Recht sprechen', deciding cases according to the law.

G148.why: The police make sure laws are followed and protect public safety.

G149.why: Denying the Holocaust is antisemitic, and in Germany it is also a crime.
G149.trap: 'Die israelische Regierung kritisieren' is tempting, but criticising a government's policy is not antisemitic in itself.

G150.why: A Gerichtsschöffe is an honorary (volunteer) judge.
G150.trap: 'Eine Person, die Jura studiert hat' is tempting, but Schöffen are ordinary citizens without legal training.

G179.why: The war in Europe officially ended with Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945.

G187.why: The flag shows black, red and gold with a hammer, compass and a wreath of wheat: that is the flag of the DDR.
G187.trap: Bundesrepublik Deutschland is tempting because of the same colours, but the West German flag has no emblem.

G188.why: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961, starting on 13 August.

G189.why: The DDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
G189.trap: 1990 is tempting because it is a key DDR year, but that was reunification, after the Wall had already fallen.

G190.why: DDR stands for Deutsche Demokratische Republik.

G200.why: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern was part of the DDR.

G222.trap: Ungarn is tempting because it is in central Europe, but Austria lies between it and Germany.
G222.trick: Nine neighbours: DK, PL, CZ, AT, CH, FR, LU, BE, NL.

G223.why: Poland borders Germany in the east, along the Oder and Neisse rivers.
G223.trap: Rumänien is tempting as an Eastern European country, but it is much further south-east.

G224.trap: Euro Union is tempting because of the currency, but the euro is only the money, and not all EU states use it.

G225.why: Austria is a German-speaking country, so it has a large German-speaking population.
G225.trap: Tschechien is tempting because German was once widely spoken there, but today it is Czech-speaking.

G226.why: Bild 2 is the EU flag: a circle of 12 gold stars on a blue background.
G226.trap: Bild 4 is tempting because it is also blue and gold, but it has no circle of stars; Bild 3 is the UN flag.

G227.why: Denmark borders Germany in the north, next to Schleswig-Holstein.

G228.why: The DDR's accession to the Bundesrepublik in 1990 is called the Deutsche Wiedervereinigung (German reunification).

G229.why: Luxembourg borders Germany in the west.
G229.trap: Spanien is tempting as a western European country, but France lies between it and Germany.

G230.trap: 6 Jahre is tempting as a near miss, but the European Parliament's term is five years, one year longer than the Bundestag's.

G231.why: 'European integration' means European states joining together, which led to the EU.
G231.trap: 'Einwanderungsstopp nach Europa' is tempting if you think of 'Integration' as a migration term, but here it means states growing together.

G232.why: In the European elections citizens elect the members of the European Parliament.
G232.trap: Die Europäische Kommission is tempting because it is a major EU body, but it is proposed by governments and confirmed by Parliament, not elected by voters.

G233.why: Czechia (Tschechien) borders Germany in the east, next to Bavaria and Saxony.
G233.trap: Bulgarien is tempting as an Eastern European country, but it is far to the south-east.

G234.why: Strasbourg is the official seat of the European Parliament, where most plenary sessions take place.
G234.trap: Berlin is tempting as Germany's capital, but the Parliament meets in Strasbourg and Brussels.

G235.why: The photo shows Mitterrand and Kohl holding hands at Verdun in 1984, a symbol of peace and reconciliation between former enemies, a core aim of the EU.

G235.trick: Hands held at Verdun = peace in Europe.

G236.why: As of October 2026 the EU has 27 member states, since the United Kingdom left in 2020; candidates such as Montenegro have not joined yet. Check before the test.
G236.trap: 25 is tempting because the EU had 25 members after 2004, but Bulgaria, Romania and Croatia joined later.

G237.why: The Treaties of Rome (1957) founded the European Economic Community (EWG).
G237.trap: 'Festlegung der Oder-Neiße-Linie' is tempting because it sounds like a big postwar treaty, but that border was settled in other treaties.

G238.why: The European Parliament works in Strasbourg (plenary sessions), Brussels (committees and extra sessions) and Luxembourg (administration).
G238.trap: 'Paris, London und Den Haag' is tempting because they are major European cities, but none of them hosts the Parliament.

G240.why: Euro notes and coins came into use on 1 January 2002.
G240.trap: 1998 is tempting because the euro was introduced as book money in 1999, but cash only came in 2002.

G241.why: Elterngeld is only paid if you apply for it at the Elterngeldstelle.
G241.trap: 'Sie bekommt automatisch Elterngeld' is tempting, but no benefit like this is paid without an application.

G242.trick: School is compulsory, Kindergarten is not.

G246.trap: 16 is tempting because some things are allowed from 16 (e.g. voting in Brandenburg), but full adulthood starts at 18.

G247.why: Mutterschutz protects pregnant women and mothers, usually six weeks before and eight weeks after the birth.
G247.trap: Elternzeit is tempting, but that is the longer parental leave either parent can take after the birth.

G248.why: Bringing up children is first of all the right and duty of the parents (Art. 6 GG).
G248.trap: Der Schulen is tempting because schools also educate, but upbringing is the parents' job first.

G249.why: Parents are mainly responsible for raising their children (Art. 6 GG).
G249.trap: Der Staat is tempting because it watches over children's welfare, but it only steps in when parents fail.

G250.why: In Germany a good education and training give you the best chances of a well-paid job.
G250.trap: 'Mitglied einer Partei' is tempting if you think of connections, but party membership is not a hiring criterion.

G251.why: Children have a right to an upbringing without violence, so hitting a child can be punished as bodily harm.
G251.trap: 'Geht nur die Familie etwas an' is tempting, but violence against children is never a private matter.
G251.trick: Hit a child, face the law.

G252.trap: 'Darf nicht wieder heiraten' is tempting if you think of religious rules, but remarrying after divorce or a spouse's death is allowed.

G253.why: After moving you must register your new address at the Einwohnermeldeamt (Bürgeramt), normally within two weeks.
G253.trap: Standesamt is tempting, but it handles births, marriages and deaths, not addresses.

G254.trap: 'Der Scheidungsprozess dauert ein Jahr' is tempting, but the year is the separation before the divorce, not the court case.

G255.why: The Jugendamt (youth welfare office) helps parents with problems raising their children.
G255.trap: Schulamt is tempting because it deals with children, but it runs schools and does not give family advice.

G256.trap: 'Eine Erlaubnis der Polizei' is tempting because the police enforce rules, but the trade or public order office is responsible.

G257.why: Adults can catch up on the Abitur at an Abendgymnasium (evening school).
G257.trap: Hochschule is tempting because it is higher education, but you normally need the Abitur before you can study there.

G258.why: The Jugendamt may take a child out of the family if it is beaten or starving, to protect it.
G258.trap: 'Es bezahlt das Kindergeld' is tempting, but Kindergeld is paid by the Familienkasse.

G259.why: The BIZ at the Bundesagentur für Arbeit helps with career choice and finding an apprenticeship (Lehrstelle).

G260.why: School is compulsory in Germany, so children must attend (Anwesenheitspflicht).
G260.trap: 'Wahlfreiheit für alle Fächer' is tempting, but most subjects are fixed by the curriculum.

G261.why: Adults can take the Abitur at an Abendgymnasium.
G261.trap: Hochschule is tempting, but you need the Abitur to study there.

G262.trap: 'Wenn ausreichende persönliche Gründe vorliegen' is tempting because it sounds reasonable, but personal reasons do not justify discrimination.

G263.why: From 14 young people can be punished for crimes, though under juvenile criminal law.
G263.trap: 'Werden wie Erwachsene behandelt' is tempting, but young people from 14 to 17 are tried under juvenile law, not adult law.

G264.why: On Rosenmontag, the highlight of Carnival, people wear colourful costumes and masks.
G264.trap: Oktoberfest is tempting because it is a big party, but people wear Dirndl and Lederhosen there, not masks.

G265.why: To get married you first go to the Standesamt (registry office).
G265.trap: Einwohnermeldeamt is tempting because it holds your personal data, but marriages are handled by the Standesamt.
G265.trick: Stand changes from ledig to verheiratet.

G266.why: The night rest period usually starts at 22:00 (10 pm).

G267.why: A 22-year-old is an adult, so her parents must respect her choice of partner.
G267.trap: 'Das Recht, die Tochter zurückzuholen' is tempting from a traditional view, but parents have no such right over an adult.

G268.why: The driving theory test can be taken in several foreign languages, more than ten in total.
G268.trap: 'Wenn sie kein Deutsch kann, darf sie keinen Führerschein haben' is tempting, but German is not required for a driving licence.

G269.why: Children from age three until they start school have a legal right to a place in a Kindergarten.
G269.trap: 'Einen Platz in einem Sportverein' is tempting because clubs are popular, but there is no legal right to it.

G270.why: The Volkshochschule offers further education courses for adults of all ages.
G270.trap: 'Nur für Rentnerinnen und Rentner' is tempting because many retirees attend, but courses are open to everyone.

G271.why: At Christmas people decorate a fir tree (Tannenbaum).
G271.trap: 'Bunte Eier verstecken' is tempting as a festive custom, but that belongs to Easter.

G272.why: Being married to two people at once is bigamy and not allowed.
G272.trap: 'Zwei Frauen leben zusammen' is tempting if you think of conservative rules, but same-sex couples are legal and can marry.

G273.why: For problems raising children you go to the Jugendamt.
G273.trap: Gesundheitsamt is tempting because it deals with families, but it handles public health.

G274.why: Opening someone else's letter on purpose breaks the secrecy of correspondence (Briefgeheimnis, Art. 10 GG).
G274.trap: Die Schweigepflicht is tempting, but that is the duty of doctors or lawyers to keep secrets.

G275.why: To apply for a divorce at the family court you need a lawyer.
G275.trap: 'Die Einwilligung der Eltern' is tempting from a traditional view, but adults divorce without their parents' consent.

G276.why: If an official treats you badly you can complain to the head of the authority.
G276.trap: 'Ich muss mir diese Behandlung gefallen lassen' is tempting if you feel powerless, but you have a right to complain.
G276.trick: Bad service? Go up the chain.

G277.why: Refusing her the job only because she is a mother is discrimination.
G277.trap: 'Kein Englisch' is tempting, but required skills are a legitimate reason to choose someone else.

G278.why: Refusing the job only because he uses a wheelchair is discrimination; an accountant can do the job sitting down.
G278.trap: 'Keine Erfahrung' is tempting, but lack of experience is a legitimate reason.
G278.trick: Skills count, the wheelchair does not.

G279.why: The Hausordnung contains rules all residents must follow, e.g. quiet hours or cleaning the stairs.
G279.trap: 'Alle Mieterinnen und Mieter im Haus' is tempting because it is about the building, but it is a set of rules, not a list of names.

G280.trap: 'Warten, bis ein anderer Bescheid kommt' is tempting, but if you do nothing the assessment becomes final.

G281.trap: Freizügigkeit is tempting because they are refused entry, but that right is about moving freely within Germany.

G282.why: German citizens who are called on to be election helpers (Wahlhelfer) must accept unless they have an important reason.
G282.trap: Lehrerin/Lehrer is tempting because it is a public role, but it is a paid job, not a compulsory honorary role.
G282.trick: Elections need helpers, and you can be called up.

G283.why: If an authority sends you a wrong bill, you lodge an objection (Widerspruch) with that authority.
G283.trap: 'Zum Finanzamt gehen' is tempting because it deals with money, but each authority handles objections to its own bills.
G283.trick: Wrong bill from a Behörde? Widerspruch.

G284.why: Because skills change fast, adults must keep learning after their training (lifelong learning).
G284.trap: 'Kinder lernen in der Schule alles' is tempting, but school cannot teach everything you will need for a whole career.

G285.why: Umsatzsteuer (VAT) is charged on goods and services, not deducted from wages.

G285.trick: Lohn = salary tax, Umsatz = sales tax.

G286.why: The Betriebsrat (works council) represents employees and helps them with problems with the employer.
G286.trap: Betriebsmanagement is tempting because of the name, but management represents the employer.

G287.why: If you want to end your job you must respect the notice period (Kündigungsfrist).
G287.trap: Die Arbeitszeit is tempting because it is part of the contract, but leaving depends on the notice period.

G288.why: Germany's special responsibility for Israel comes from the Nazi crimes against Jews, above all the Holocaust.

G289.why: Rejecting him only because of his skin colour is discrimination.
G289.trap: 'Seine Deutschkenntnisse sind zu gering' is tempting, but language skills can be a legitimate job requirement.
G289.trick: Skin colour is never a reason.

G290.why: A new item that does not work can be returned to the seller with a complaint (reklamieren); you have a statutory warranty.
G290.trap: 'Das Gerät ungefragt austauschen' is tempting, but you cannot just swap it yourself without the shop's agreement.

G292.why: Religious tolerance means everyone may believe what they want (Art. 4 GG).

G293.trap: 'Einen Tannenbaum schmücken' is tempting as a festive custom, but that belongs to Christmas.

G294.why: Pentecost (Pfingsten) is a Christian holiday, 50 days after Easter.
G294.trap: 'Bayerischer Brauch' is tempting because Bavaria has many holidays, but Pfingsten is celebrated throughout Germany.

G295.why: European and German culture has been shaped above all by Christianity.

G296.why: The four weeks before Christmas are Advent (Adventszeit).

G297.why: Turkey is the largest country of origin when you count immigrants and their descendants (about 2.6 million in the 2025 Mikrozensus). As of October 2026, Poland has slightly more first-generation immigrants, so the catalogue answer is Türkei. Check before the test.
